chunks.text: Modularity divides a system into modules that can be developed and changed separately. Coupling measures how strongly modules depend on each other. Cohesion measures how closely the elements inside one module belong together.
Information hiding keeps design decisions that are likely to change inside one module. Low coupling and high cohesion improve maintainability, because a change stays local to one module.
A class diagram shows the classes of a system and the relationships between them. A component diagram shows how larger parts of the system are connected through interfaces.
Equivalence partitioning divides the input domain into classes whose members are expected to behave alike.
Boundary value analysis selects test inputs at the edges of the classes found by equivalence partitioning, where faults are often found.
Branch coverage measures whether each decision outcome has been executed by the tests. Full branch coverage does not show that every path through the code has been executed.
